column1: # Every suite in the tree, and what runs it. Read by bin/check-suites.
# The tree holds 45 top-level suites and the merge gate ran seven of them. The
# other 38 were named by nothing: not by ci/suites.txt, not by bin/nightly-full,
# not by the worker, which is agent-driven and runs what an agent remembers. A
# suite nothing names is a suite nobody is told about when it goes red, and two
# of them were red on the trunk when this file was written -- neither rotted,
# both with an input that had drifted, and nothing anywhere said so.
# This registry exists so that the question "should this be in the gate?" has a
# written answer per suite rather than an implicit one. bin/check-suites holds
# it closed both ways: a suite in the tree with no row here fails, and a row
# here naming a file that is gone fails. The gate tier is held one-to-one with
# ci/suites.txt, so the two files cannot disagree.
# tier:
#   gate        runs in ci/gate.sh before a merge. Fast, offline, deterministic,
#               and needing no input outside the checkout. A gate suite that
#               depends on a build product or a mirror would block every merge
#               on the state of one machine.
#   report      should run and be reported, but not gate: it needs a toolchain,
#               a build product, a vendor input or a live el8, any of which can
#               be legitimately absent. bin/nightly-full runs these; an absent
#               input makes it not-checked rather than failed, the distinction
#               test/t3-regen.sh already draws for spikes.
#   standalone  never automated, with the reason in the note.
# needs: a path that must exist for the suite to be runnable, or - if none.
# A new suite cannot land undesignated. bin/check-suites fails when a suite in
# the tree has no row here, so the author writes a tier and a reason at the
# moment of writing rather than leaving it to whoever notices later. There is
# deliberately no default: an unregistered suite is an error, not a `report`,
# because a default is how a thing stops being thought about. The same check
# holds every `t/` directory to having at least one registered entry point, so
# a runner under a name this file's conventions do not anticipate is caught
# too.
